name: Spanish Bistre
lede: Spanish Bistre is a dull, olive-leaning brown named for bistre, a soot-based pigment, and it shows up in nearly three percent of our museum archive.

sections.title: A pigment word, borrowed
sections.body: Our classifier files Spanish Bistre as a pigment, mineral or dye word, built on "bistre," the old brown wash artists made from chimney soot [1]. The "Spanish" in front is not explained in the sources we hold; it names no specific regional recipe here [1]. The nearest named colors on file are [[dusty-hazel-tone]], [[dark-citrine]], [[ugly-brown]] and [[khaki-brown]], at 3.5, 5, 5, 5, 5.2 and 5.2 ΔE [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, as photographed, this color covers five percent or more of the canvas in 700 of them, about 2.9 percent[2]. Its earliest dated appearance is a 1410 altarpiece, *Coronation of the Virgin*, and it peaks in the 1710s, in 12 of 169 paintings, over twice the archive's average rate, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2].

Paulus Potter carries it in nearly a third of his dated paintings, and it leans toward eighteenth and nineteenth-century landscape and still life more than earlier work [2]. It most often sits as a mid-tone or highlight rather than a shadow, and shares canvases with [[olive]], [[khaki]] and [[mustard|Mustard]] far more than chance would predict [2].
